tagline: How a group of machines agrees on one thing even when some crash: majorities, terms, leader election and log replication in Raft.
:: simple
**Consensus** means a group of nodes agree on a value (who is leader, the next entry in a log, whether a transaction commits), even if some nodes crash or messages are delayed. It is the building block under almost every reliable cluster: etcd and Kubernetes, ZooKeeper, Consul, the metadata of many databases and queues.

The core trick is the **majority** (a quorum). With 3 nodes, a majority is 2. With 5 nodes, 3. Any two majorities share at least one member, so two different decisions can never both get a majority. That is why clusters use odd sizes and why 3 nodes tolerate 1 failure and 5 tolerate 2. A cluster that loses its majority **stops accepting writes** instead of guessing. That feels like an outage, but it is the safe behavior.

### Raft in plain words
Raft is a consensus algorithm designed to be understandable. At any moment each node is a **follower**, a **candidate** or the **leader**.
1. Followers expect regular "heartbeats" from a leader.
2. If a follower hears nothing for a random while (the *election timeout*), it becomes a candidate, adds 1 to its **term** number, and asks the others for votes.
3. Each node votes once per term. A candidate with a majority becomes the leader.
4. Clients talk to the leader. It appends each command to its log, sends it to the followers, and once a **majority** has stored it, the entry is **committed** and applied.

Try this live in the [simulated 3-node cluster](cluster.html): kill the leader and watch a new election.
> A **term** is Raft's logical clock. A message from an older term is rejected. That single rule is what stops an old leader that comes back from overriding the new one.
:: mid
### Election details
- Election timeouts are randomized (for example 150 to 300 ms) so nodes rarely become candidates at the same moment. If votes split, the term ends with no leader and a new one starts.
- A node only votes for a candidate whose log is **at least as up-to-date** as its own (higher last term, or same term and at least as long). This guarantees a new leader already holds every committed entry.
- Whenever any node sees a higher term it steps down to follower and adopts that term.

### Log replication
The leader sends `AppendEntries` with the index and term of the entry just before the new ones. A follower accepts only if its log matches at that point; if not, it rejects and the leader steps back until the logs agree, then overwrites the follower's extra entries. So followers' logs are forced to match the leader's. The leader advances the **commit index** when a majority holds an entry **from its own term**; followers learn the commit index from later heartbeats.

### What happens in a partition (3 nodes)
Suppose the leader is cut off from the other two. The two followers stop hearing heartbeats, one becomes a candidate in a higher term and wins with 2 of 3 votes. Now there are two nodes that think they lead: the old leader (old term, no majority) and the new one. The old leader can append writes but they will **never commit** because it cannot reach a majority. When the partition heals it sees the higher term, steps down, and its uncommitted entries are **discarded** and replaced. A client that was told "ok" before commit has been lied to, which is why clients should only trust acknowledgment after commit.

### Reads
A leader that has been partitioned may still believe it leads and answer reads with stale data. Safe designs make the leader confirm it still has a majority before answering (a read index or a lease), or accept stale reads on purpose.
:: complex
### Paxos and friends
**Paxos** (Lamport) came first and is the theoretical foundation. A proposer runs two phases (prepare/promise, accept/accepted) against acceptors; a value chosen by a majority stays chosen. Multi-Paxos repeats it for a log. It is correct but famously hard to implement; **Raft** (Ongaro and Ousterhout, 2014) restructured the same ideas into leader election, log replication and safety, which is why most new systems use it. **ZAB** (ZooKeeper) and **Viewstamped Replication** are close relatives. Consensus that must survive lying nodes needs **BFT** protocols (PBFT, Tendermint) with 3f + 1 nodes to tolerate f Byzantine ones.

### Safety properties worth stating
- **Election safety**: at most one leader per term.
- **Leader append-only**: a leader never overwrites or deletes its own entries.
- **Log matching**: if two logs have an entry with the same index and term, they are identical up to that point.
- **Leader completeness**: a committed entry appears in the logs of all future leaders.
- **State machine safety**: no two nodes apply different commands at the same index.

### Fencing, leases, and the pause problem
Timeouts assume bounded pauses. A process frozen by garbage collection or a VM migration can wake up after its lease expired and still think it is leader. Defense: every write to shared storage carries the **term or fencing token**, and the storage rejects anything older than the highest it has seen.

### Membership and operations
Adding or removing nodes safely needs a special procedure (joint consensus or one-at-a-time changes). Disk fsync latency bounds your commit speed, so consensus clusters want fast, local SSDs. Never run a 2-node "cluster" and expect failover: it has no majority after one failure. Use 3, or 2 plus a witness. Keep consensus clusters in a single region or a low-latency link, because every commit waits for a majority round trip.

### Two-phase commit is not consensus
**2PC** coordinates a transaction across several databases: prepare (everyone votes yes/no), then commit. If the coordinator crashes after prepare, participants are stuck holding locks until it returns (it **blocks**). Consensus-based systems replicate the coordinator's decision to avoid that single point of failure (Spanner does this with Paxos groups plus 2PC).

### Security angle
Whoever can join the cluster or forge a vote controls it. etcd holds all Kubernetes secrets, so its client and peer ports must use mutual TLS and sit on a private network. Take regular, tested snapshots. An attacker who can partition or slow the network can force repeated elections: availability attacks need no exploit at all. Alert on frequent term changes.
:: lab
style: shell
host: etcd-ops
user: sre
cwd: /home/sre
:: brief
A 3-node consensus cluster (`n1`, `n2`, `n3`) had a short network partition. Afterwards a developer reports that a write they were told succeeded is missing.

Investigate in `~/cluster`: the three node logs. Find the write that was accepted by the old leader but **never committed** and was thrown away when the partition healed. Submit its **log index**.
:: answer
12
:: hint
Look at who was leader before the partition and which term the new leader got elected in: `grep -h "became leader" ~/cluster/*.log`.
:: hint
The old leader kept appending while cut off. Compare its last `append` lines with its `truncate` line after it rejoined.
:: solution
n1 was leader in term 4. After the partition, n2 and n3 elected n2 in term 5 with 2 of 3 votes. n1 still thought it led term 4 and appended `SET balance=50` at index 12, but it could not reach a majority, so the entry was never committed. When the link healed, n1 saw term 5, stepped down, and **truncated index 12** to match n2's log. The developer was told "ok" because the client library treated the leader's append as success. Fix: acknowledge only after commit, and retry against the new leader with an idempotency key.
:: verify
grep -h truncate ~/cluster/n1.log
:: file /home/sre/cluster/n1.log

08:10:41 term=5 heartbeat ok from n2 (leader)
